promptText: What is the "first rule of ARIA"?
options: Don't use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute already provides the semantics and behavior you need
Always add role and aria-label to every interactive element, even native ones, to be extra explicit
ARIA attributes should only be used inside a <div>, never on semantic elements like <button>
Use aria-hidden on every element that is not currently visible on screen
explanation: The first rule of ARIA is to prefer native HTML whenever it already gives you the needed semantics and behavior. ARIA only changes how an element is announced -- it adds no keyboard handling, focus behavior, or built-in interaction, so reaching for it when a native element would already work just adds redundant complexity and risk.

promptText:
A developer builds a clickable card as `
Save
` instead of a `
options: Keyboard focusability, activation via Enter and Space, and a visible focus indicator -- all of which must be manually reimplemented on the div and are easy to get subtly wrong
Nothing else is missing; role="button" alone is functionally equivalent to a real button element
Only the CSS styling differs; behavior is identical between a div and a button by default
The div will automatically inherit tabIndex and keyboard handling from its parent form element
explanation: A native <button> ships an entire accessibility contract: it's in the tab order, fires on both Enter and Space, and shows a focus ring, all for free. A <div onClick> has none of that -- it isn't focusable, doesn't respond to keyboard activation, and needs manually added tabIndex, keydown handling, and focus styles to even approximate the native behavior, and it's easy to miss edge cases.

promptText: An input has both a visible `<label>` associated via `htmlFor`/`id` AND an `aria-label` attribute set to a different string. Which one determines the input's accessible name?
options: The aria-label value, because aria-label takes priority over a native label association in the accessible-name computation order
The native <label> text, because visible labels always override any ARIA attribute
Both are concatenated together into one combined accessible name
Neither is used; the input falls back to its placeholder text instead
explanation: The accessible-name computation resolves in priority order: aria-labelledby first, then aria-label, then a native label association, then the element's own text content. Since aria-label is present, it wins over the native <label> even though the label is visible -- which is exactly why mismatched aria-label and visible label text is a real, confusing bug (voice-control users saying the visible label text won't match the announced name).

promptText: Which tabIndex value should NEVER be used, and why?
options: A positive value (e.g. tabIndex={5}), because it hijacks the natural DOM-order tab sequence and creates a maintenance nightmare as the page evolves
tabIndex={0}, because it removes an element from the tab order entirely
tabIndex={-1}, because it is not supported by any modern browser
Any tabIndex value on a <button>, because native buttons cannot accept a tabIndex attribute
explanation: tabIndex={0} places an element in the natural tab order at its DOM position; tabIndex={-1} makes it focusable only via script (useful for roving focus or focus targets). A positive tabIndex overrides the natural order with an explicit numeric sequence, which is fragile and desyncs from DOM/reading order as the page changes -- it is universally considered an anti-pattern.

promptText: A form shows a red border on an invalid field but no icon or text change. What WCAG issue does this create, and how does it differ from a contrast ratio problem?
options: It conveys information (validity) by color alone (WCAG 1.4.1), which is a distinct criterion from contrast (1.4.3) -- a colorblind user may not perceive the red at all regardless of how strong the contrast ratio is
It is purely a contrast ratio problem (1.4.3), and increasing the red's contrast against the background would fully resolve it
There is no accessibility issue since red is a widely recognized convention for errors in every culture and visual condition
The issue only matters for AAA compliance, not for the AA level most sites are required to meet
explanation: Use-of-color (1.4.1) and contrast (1.4.3) are separate WCAG success criteria that are commonly conflated. A red-only error indicator fails 1.4.1 regardless of how high its contrast ratio is, because a colorblind user may not distinguish red from the surrounding UI at all -- the fix is pairing color with text or an icon, not just boosting contrast.

promptText: A team runs axe DevTools on every page and considers their app fully accessible once it reports zero violations. What is the flaw in this approach?
options: Automated tools like axe only catch a subset of accessibility issues (roughly a third) -- they can detect a missing alt attribute but not whether the alt text is meaningful, so manual keyboard and screen-reader testing is still required
axe DevTools only works on pages built with React and produces false results on plain HTML pages
Automated tools cannot check color contrast at all, so a separate manual process is the only way to verify contrast ratios
Zero violations from axe is a legally binding certification of full WCAG AAA compliance
explanation: Automated tools are excellent at catching mechanical issues (missing labels, invalid ARIA, contrast ratios) but cannot judge subjective usability -- whether alt text actually describes the image meaningfully, whether a screen-reader user can actually complete a task, or whether the keyboard experience feels reasonable. A layered approach combining automation with real keyboard-only and screen-reader testing is the only reliable coverage.

promptText: A modal implementation correctly traps Tab/Shift+Tab inside the dialog and closes on Escape, but users report that after closing the modal, keyboard focus ends up on the document body with no clear next step. What is missing?
options: Restoring focus to the element that originally opened the modal (the trigger) when the modal closes -- one of the most commonly forgotten steps in a hand-rolled modal implementation
An aria-modal="true" attribute, since without it Escape cannot close the dialog at all
A role="presentation" on the backdrop element, which is required for focus to return anywhere after closing
Converting the modal to use position: fixed instead of position: absolute for its backdrop
explanation: A correct modal must remember document.activeElement before opening and call .focus() on it when the modal closes. Without this, closing the modal leaves focus nowhere meaningful (often reset to the body), stranding keyboard and screen-reader users -- this is called out as the single most-forgotten step in accessible modal implementations.

promptText:
A toast notification component conditionally renders an entire `
{message}
` only when there is a message to show. Screen reader users report that toasts are sometimes never announced. What is the bug?
options: The live region and its text are mounted together in the same render; screen readers announce a live region's diff after it already exists in the DOM, so mounting the container and its content simultaneously can cause the announcement to be missed -- the region should stay permanently mounted with only its text changing
aria-live="polite" is the wrong value and should always be "assertive" for toast notifications to be announced reliably
The bug is that toasts must use role="alert" instead of aria-live, since aria-live does not support text content at all
Screen readers cannot announce any content that changes via React state, regardless of how the live region is structured
explanation: Screen readers announce changes to an existing live region's contents. If the whole region (container + text) is conditionally mounted at once, some screen readers miss the announcement because there was no prior 'empty' state to diff against. The fix is to keep the live region permanently in the DOM and toggle only its text via state.

promptText: A skip link targets `<main id="main">` with `href="#main"` but no tabIndex attribute on the main element. What problem can this cause in some browsers?
options: Activating the skip link scrolls the page to #main but does not move keyboard focus there, since <main> is not natively focusable -- the very next Tab press then starts again from the top of the page
The skip link will fail to render at all without a tabIndex on its target
Browsers will throw a console error because href="#main" requires the target to have role="main" explicitly set
This has no effect since all landmark elements are automatically focusable by default in every browser
explanation: Jumping to an anchor scrolls the page in some browsers without actually moving keyboard focus, since <main> isn't natively focusable. Giving the target tabIndex={-1} makes it programmatically focusable so the skip link's jump actually relocates focus, not just the visual scroll position -- otherwise the next Tab press resumes from the top of the document, defeating the skip link's purpose.

promptText: A React single-page app built with a client-side router works fine visually, but screen-reader users report they have no idea when navigation to a new page has happened. What causes this, and what MPA behavior is being lost?
options: Client-side route changes only swap rendered components without a full page load, so the browser's native behavior of resetting focus to the top and announcing the new page never happens -- this must be recreated manually (e.g., focusing the new page's heading and/or using a live-region route announcer)
The issue only occurs when using React Router specifically; all other routing libraries handle this automatically with zero extra code
Screen readers cannot detect any DOM changes made by JavaScript, so this problem is fundamentally unfixable in any SPA
The fix is to force a full page reload on every navigation, which is the only way to restore the expected screen-reader behavior
explanation: In a traditional multi-page app, a full page load naturally resets focus to the top of the document and screen readers announce the new page. Client-side routing only swaps components in place, so neither of those things happens automatically -- the standard fix is to focus the new page's heading (with tabIndex={-1}) after each navigation and/or maintain a visually-hidden live region that announces the new page title.

promptText: A modal sets `aria-hidden="true"` on the rest of the app while open, but a background `<button>` is still reachable by pressing Tab even though a screen reader will not announce it. What is the correct fix, and why does it work where aria-hidden alone did not?
options: Use the inert attribute on the background container instead -- inert removes the subtree from the accessibility tree AND makes it unfocusable, whereas aria-hidden only affects the accessibility tree and has no effect on tab order or focusability
Add role="presentation" to the background container, which specifically disables tab order for all descendant elements
aria-hidden="true" is already sufficient and the reported Tab-reachability is expected, correct behavior
Wrap every background focusable element individually in aria-live="off" to remove it from the tab sequence
explanation: aria-hidden only removes an element's subtree from the accessibility tree -- it does not change focusability, so a background button remains reachable by keyboard even though it's invisible to a screen reader, creating a confusing 'reachable but silent' bug. The native inert attribute solves both problems in one step: it removes the subtree from the accessibility tree AND makes it unfocusable and unclickable, which is why it has largely replaced hand-rolled aria-hidden + tabIndex=-1 polyfills.

promptText: A page has two `<nav>` elements, neither with an aria-label, plus a single `<main>` and a single `<header>`. What accessibility problem does a screen-reader user encounter when opening the landmarks list?
options: The landmarks list shows two identical, indistinguishable "navigation" entries, since neither nav has a distinct label to differentiate them -- multiple landmarks of the same type are fine as long as each gets a unique aria-label
Having two <nav> elements is invalid HTML and the browser will silently ignore the second one entirely
The page cannot have more than one landmark of any kind, so this will cause the header and main landmarks to disappear
Screen readers will merge the two nav elements into a single combined navigation region automatically
explanation: Multiple navigation (or region/complementary) landmarks are perfectly valid and common, but each needs a distinct aria-label so they're distinguishable when a screen-reader user brings up the landmarks list -- without labels, two navs both show up as generic 'navigation, navigation' entries, which defeats the purpose of landmark navigation for the exact users it's meant to help.

promptText:
A component renders `
Save
` with no other changes. According to the five rules of ARIA, what specifically is wrong, and what does adding `role="button"` actually accomplish versus what it fails to accomplish?
options: role="button" only changes how the element is ANNOUNCED to assistive technology -- it does not make the div focusable, does not wire up Enter/Space activation, and does not add a visible focus indicator, all of which must still be added manually; this is a rule-3 violation (interactive ARIA widgets must be keyboard-operable)
role="button" fully replicates native <button> behavior including focusability and keyboard activation, so the code is already correct as written
The div will throw a runtime error because role="button" cannot be combined with an onClick handler in React
This is a violation of the rule against changing native semantics, since a <div> already has an implicit role that role="button" is illegally overriding
explanation: ARIA is a promise to assistive technology, not an implementation -- role="button" makes the element announced as a button, but a screen-reader or keyboard user still cannot reach or activate it, because there's no tabIndex, no keydown handler for Enter/Space, and no focus style. This is exactly why 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA': the role creates an expectation (keyboard operability, per rule 3) that the code fails to fulfill, actively misleading assistive-tech users.

promptText: Given `Billing addressrequired`, what accessible name will the input actually get, and what common mistake does this illustrate?
options: "required Billing address" -- aria-labelledby concatenates the referenced elements' text in the exact order the ids are listed, so reversing the id order (as done here) reverses the announced name, which is a real, easy-to-miss authoring bug
"Billing address required", because aria-labelledby always concatenates in DOM order regardless of how the ids are listed in the attribute
Only "Billing address", because aria-labelledby ignores every id after the first one listed
An empty string, because aria-labelledby cannot reference more than one id at a time
explanation: aria-labelledby accepts a space-separated list of ids and concatenates their text content in the order the ids are listed in the attribute value -- not DOM order. Since the attribute here lists "req lbl" (req first), the announced name is "required Billing address", not the more natural "Billing address required" -- a subtle ordering bug that only shows up when you actually listen to the announcement.

promptText: A toolbar with 6 buttons gives every button `tabIndex={0}` so a user can reach each one, relying only on Tab to move between them. Per the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide's keyboard model for composite widgets, what is wrong with this approach compared to roving tabindex?
options: Composite widgets should be a single Tab stop, with arrow keys moving focus WITHIN the widget (roving tabindex: one item at tabIndex={0}, the rest at tabIndex={-1}); giving every button tabIndex={0} forces the user to Tab through all 6 individually, breaking the expected 'Tab between widgets, arrows within a widget' keyboard model
tabIndex={0} on multiple sibling elements is invalid HTML and will cause the browser to only focus the first one, ignoring the rest
There is no meaningful difference; roving tabindex and giving every item tabIndex={0} produce identical user experiences in every screen reader
Roving tabindex is only a performance optimization for large lists and has no bearing on the actual keyboard interaction model
explanation: The APG keyboard model for composite widgets like toolbars, tabs, and menus treats the whole widget as ONE stop in the page's Tab sequence, with arrow keys moving focus among the widget's own items (roving tabindex: exactly one item is tabIndex={0} at a time, the rest are tabIndex={-1}, and arrow keys move which one is 0). Giving every button tabIndex={0} makes Tab step through each one individually, which is slower and violates the keyboard contract users and screen readers expect from that widget type.
